checkpoints.title: Build the local sensing layer of an IoT system

blocks.title: Central question
paragraphs: How does a change in physical temperature become a live digital temperature display in LabVIEW?

You are building the first sensing node for an Internet of Things temperature-monitoring system. Before data can be sent to the cloud, the local system must correctly sense temperature, convert a physical change into voltage, acquire that voltage using Arduino, and display a meaningful temperature value in LabVIEW.
This lab focuses on the local sensing layer, not yet the cloud layer.

steps.label: Divider voltage
steps.detail: A voltage appears at the junction.

paragraphs: LabVIEW does not directly measure temperature. Arduino reads a voltage, and LabVIEW uses the course-provided thermistor conversion VI or instructor-provided sensor parameters to infer temperature.

blocks.title: By the end of this lab, you should be able to...
items: **Sensor model** — Explain how a thermistor changes resistance with temperature.
**Voltage divider** — Explain why the circuit converts resistance change into measurable voltage.
**Arduino role** — Identify how Arduino acquires analog sensor data from A0.
**LabVIEW LINX** — Identify how LabVIEW communicates with Arduino.
**VI building** — Build controls, indicators, arithmetic functions, and unit conversion logic.
**SubVI reuse** — Convert a VI into a reusable SubVI with an icon and connector pane.
**Live display** — Read voltage, convert temperature, and display Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin.
**Troubleshooting** — Diagnose hardware, firmware, wiring, and LabVIEW block-diagram faults.

checkpoints.title: Build a basic temperature-conversion VI
intro: Create a LabVIEW VI that converts degrees Celsius to degrees Fahrenheit. Save it as `Convert C to F.vi`.

blocks.summary: How to build it: Front Panel
items: Open LabVIEW and create a blank VI.
Add a numeric control labelled `deg C`.
Add a numeric indicator labelled `deg F`.

blocks.summary: How to build it: Block Diagram
items: Use Multiply, Add, numeric constant `1.8`, and numeric constant `32.0`.
Wire the Celsius control through `F = 1.8C + 32`.
Run the VI with several values before trusting it.

blocks.title: Think it through
items: Which object is the input?
Which object is the output?
Where is the equation represented in the block diagram?
What happens if a wire is missing?
How does LabVIEW dataflow differ from line-by-line text programming?
Why should you test 0 °C and 100 °C before trusting the VI?

checkpoints.title: Turn your conversion into a reusable SubVI
intro: Reopen `Convert C to F.vi` and convert it into a SubVI. A SubVI is a reusable block that hides internal details while exposing defined inputs and outputs.

items: Save a backup copy of the working Celsius-to-Fahrenheit VI.
Open the VI front panel and confirm the control is named `deg C` and the indicator is named `deg F`.
Open the icon editor and create a simple, readable icon that communicates C to F conversion.
Open the connector pane and choose a two-terminal pattern.
Assign the left terminal to `deg C` and the right terminal to `deg F`.
Turn on Context Help and hover over the SubVI icon to confirm the terminals are labelled correctly.
Save the SubVI, then place it in a new test VI and verify 0, 25, and 100 degrees Celsius.

blocks.title: Build focus
paragraphs: Use the instructor-provided schematic and bench hardware to identify the thermistor, fixed resistor, 5 V, GND, and the divider junction that feeds Arduino A0.
Sketch your own wiring map before powering. The goal is to understand the signal path rather than copy a picture.

blocks.title: Confirm placement before power
paragraphs: Confirm the exact thermistor and resistor placement with your instructor or the course-provided schematic before powering the Arduino. Reversing the thermistor and fixed resistor may reverse the temperature-voltage relationship.

blocks.title: Safe recovery sequence
paragraphs: If the reading is missing or implausible, disconnect USB power before moving wires. Verify 5 V, GND, the A0 divider junction, thermistor seating, and the 10 kΩ resistor row; then confirm LINX firmware, serial port, and analog channel 0. Change one item at a time and retest with a measurement or inspection.

checkpoints.title: Read the sensor and test the temperature response
intro: Create a main VI that opens a LINX connection, reads Arduino analog channel 0, sends the voltage to the course-provided thermistor conversion VI, reuses your C-to-F SubVI, lets the user select Celsius or Fahrenheit, displays the result on a thermometer indicator, repeats inside a while loop, stops with a Stop button, and closes LINX after the loop ends.

blocks.alt: Annotated LabVIEW LINX block diagram identifying the serial connection, analog read, digital write, timing, stop control, error wire, while loop, and close function
blocks.caption: Use this annotated dataflow reference to distinguish connection setup, repeated measurement and output logic, controlled stopping, and resource cleanup.

paragraphs: Add temperature scale switch, thermometer indicator, serial port control or constant, and Stop button.
Organize dataflow left to right: open, read, convert, select, display, close.
Use LINX Open with the Arduino serial port. Keep it outside the while loop.
Use LINX Analog Read with Analog Channel constant set to `0`.
Use the course-provided thermistor conversion VI or instructor-provided sensor parameters.
Use your C-to-F SubVI and a Select function controlled by the Temp Scale switch.
Place repeated measurement and display code inside the loop so data updates live.
Wire the Stop button to the loop condition and place LINX Close after the loop.
Run the VI, touch or warm the thermistor, observe response, then stop with the Stop button.

paragraphs: **Glossary — key terms**
A resistor whose resistance changes with temperature.
Opposition to electric current, measured in Ω.
Two resistive elements that create a measurable junction voltage.
A continuously varying voltage value.
A microcontroller input that measures voltage and converts it to a number.
Analog input channel 0 on the Arduino.
Analog-to-digital converter.
A graphical programming environment.
Virtual Instrument, a LabVIEW program.
The user-facing controls and indicators of a VI.
The graphical program logic of a VI.
A LabVIEW input object.
A LabVIEW output display object.
A reusable VI used as a block inside another VI.
The terminal mapping that defines SubVI inputs and outputs.
LabVIEW toolkit for communicating with supported hardware such as Arduino.
The communication port used by the computer to talk to Arduino.
A repeated LabVIEW structure that continues until a stop condition is met.
A controlled way to end a running VI.
An emergency stop that can interrupt cleanup logic and should not be the normal stop method.
A temperature scale based on water freezing at 0 and boiling at 100 under standard conditions.
A temperature scale where `F = 1.8C + 32`.
An absolute temperature scale where `K = C + 273.15`.
Relating measured signals to meaningful physical values.
Small variation in readings caused by circuit, environment, or measurement limits.
The time required for a sensor reading to approach a new stable value.
A local device that senses a physical condition and can later send data to a network or cloud system.
